thread.title: Investors have been 'mindlessly' following this hot-stock strategy all year | MyFXinfo

title: Investors have been 'mindlessly' following this hot-stock strategy all year | MyFXinfo
text:
AAPL, +2.20% due the week after.
While plenty of blue chips will report between now and then, the cadre of techy names referred to as FAANGs, will draw special attention from investors, as they have been the group—by dint of their market value and investor lust for growth—that has sustained the current bull-market rally, even if 2018 is looking decidedly more volatile.
Outside of Tuesday’s burst higher, the broader downturn in equity markets, and FAANG names specifically, has created a degree of uneasiness within the FAANG stalwarts.
Thus far investors have been of two camps: The FOMO, or fear of missing out, set, who have helped to drive stocks higher, with those market participants piling on to companies that have been enjoying better-than-average share-price gains. And those on the FOIAE, or fear of it all ending, side. That is those who fret that each political conflagration or pricey sector could be the final undoing of a decadelong bull market.
Only time will tell who is right.
That leads us to our call of the day , from Kevin Muir of the Macro Tourist blog , who raises questions over an investment strategy that has been red-hot over the past year, but which may be showing signs of decline. Take a look at his chart, which shows the biggest factors that have been driving U.S. stock performance over the past year: Bloomberg, Macro Tourist
Take note of the factor which has crested to the top, and by a pretty big margin: three-month target-price changes. “This means that mindlessly following analyst 3-month target price changes was the smartest strategy over the past year from this list,” wrote Muir.
The next biggest factor is U.S. Momentum, which Muir is a strategy by which investors buy the biggest risers over the last 12 months and selling their losers. “What about stuff like Price/Earnings or Price/Book ratios? Where are those fundamental factors? Surely, just chasing the hot stock can’t be a portfolio strategy,” he argues, but yeah that is what’s been working for investors. Buying momentum stocks.
At the bottom of that above chart is one definitely not-hot strategy—value, which has gotten no breaks this year, Muir notes.
Over the past two-years that momentum strategy looks like a clear winner, but he’s more interested in this chart that shows what’s been going on over the last 12 months. Bloomberg, Macro Tourist
In short, momentum has been relinquishing ground or at least losing, well, momentum.
“’Momentum’ is no longer being rewarded quite as heavily, and in fact, during the latest equity market sell off, the stocks that had performed the best over the past year led the move to the downside,” said Muir. End of that trend friend? We shall see. The market
